newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels battle Hutus, oppose international force.
newsitem.headline: Rebels battle Hutus, oppose international force.

text.p: Rebels battled Hutu foes in eastern Zaire on Thursday and dismissed the limited mandate of a planned multinational military force as "useless".
The Canadian-led force with a powerful U.S. contingent is expected on the ground within days. But both countries say their troops will not separate Hutu fighters from ordinary refugees.
Fighting raged around the eastern Zaire town of Goma for six hours as Tutsi rebels took on exiled Rwandan Hutu former soldiers and militiamen before the international force arrives.

"I am opposed to any force that is not neutral, and a force that comes here without a mandate to separate the Interahamwe and the refugees is unfeasible, impractical and useless," rebel chief Laurent Kabila told a news conference in Goma.
Kabila was referring to Interahamwe militiamen who helped lead the genocide of up to one million people in Rwanda in 1994 and are intimidating refugees in Zaire against returning home.

Aid workers say that without taking on the thousands of armed Hutus, who are accused by the rebels of using refugees as human shields, the mission would be a failure as it will not lead to mass repatriation.

The rebels and the mainly Tutsi leaderships of Rwanda and Burundi fear that the Hutu fighters will be in effect protected by the multinational force and the 1.2 million refugees will stay in eastern Zaire.
But after four weeks of mounting crisis, Western powers readied to send in troops while stressing their mission would be strictly humanitarian to avoid being bogged down in fighting.

The rebels holding a strip of eastern Zaire are also opposed to French involvement in the international force, arguing France backs Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and supported the Hutu-led government in Rwanda before the genocide.

Underlining the hazards ahead for the U.N.-endorsed intervention force, firing from mortar, anti-aircraft and machineguns boomed around the teeming Mugunga camp 10 km (six miles) west of rebel-held Goma on Rwanda's border.
Some estimates say Mugunga remains home to 400,000 Hutu refugees, or one-third of the Rwandan and Burundian Hutus scattered in eastern Zaire by a month-long Tutsi-led revolt.
After arriving by boat in Goma with 800 other people fleeing fighting and cholera, Zairean Lwaboshi Menne quoted Interahamwe gunmen as saying they would take on the multinational force.

"If foreign troops come here the Interahamwe are saying they will fight them before they run," said Menne after they blocked his escape route by road. "They were everywhere...on the roads and in the bush."
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said Africa-bound U.S. troops would be armed to protect themselves but not to conduct combat operations while helping deliver aid to the refugees.
Perry said in Washington the projected ground force of as many as 1,000 U.S. troops, part of the multinational expedition, would have "robust" rules of engagement to protect itself.
"We are not planning a mission to go in and disarm factions or to separate the military from refugees," he said.
Canada said on Thursday Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril would head the force. An advance team of Canadian troops was to leave for Zaire later on Thursday to assess the situation.
Eritrea, one of only seven African states which have tentatively agreed to join the force, backed out on Thursday.
Foreign Miinister Petros Solomon told Reuters in Asmara his country opposed Ottawa's leadership because of Canada's recent chequered record in peacekeeping in Somalia and Rwanda.
A U.S. military assessment team of 37 arrived in the Rwandan capital Kigali from Uganda on Thursday to prepare for the dispatch of the several thousand U.S. troops to central Africa.
"We are here to conduct an initial assessment for a possible mission... either unilateral or multilateral," Major-General Edward Smith, commander of the South European Task Force, told reporters.
The first could leave for Africa as early as next week.

But even before they set foot in the Great Lakes region, home to an explosive cocktail of mixed ethnic and political conflicts, even aid officials who had called for intervention questioned whether it could succeed with such limited aims.
The head of the U.N.'s food aid arm said on Thursday the force must separate "the bad guys with the guns" from starving refugees or its mission would have to be repeated.

Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme, said while the first step would be seeing no weapons interfered with humanitarian work, ultimately fighters would have to be disarmed.

"The step necessary for peace in the long term is disarmament but if we're talking about keeping people alive and feeding people today we would want to separate the bad guys with the guns from the people who need to live today," she said.
Rwanda, where Tutsi rebels drove out the Interhamwe and Hutu troops in 1994, also said the force was doomed to failure.

"This is a false start. As long as the international force is not prepared to disarm the ex-FAR (army troops) and the Interahamwe its objectives will not be achieved," Seth Kamanzi, an adviser to the Rwandan president, said.
France, distrusted by Tutsis in the region for financial and military support to Rwanda's former Hutu government, said it hoped the first foreign troops would be in Zaire by the weekend.
